html:
If you run a contractor limited company, do you actually know how much of your profit goes to HMRC - and how much you could legally keep? Most contractors have a rough idea of the 19% and 25% rates, but the real complexity sits underneath those headline figures. Your IR35 status, the way you extract profit, and the expenses you claim all combine to produce a corporation tax bill that can vary dramatically from one contractor to the next, even on identical turnover.

Working out corporation tax as a contractor is more complicated than it looks. This guide gives you a plain-English walkthrough of exactly how your tax is calculated and what you can do to reduce it. By the end, you will understand three things that matter most: your IR35 status and how it reshapes your taxable profit, the allowable expenses that reduce your bill before you even reach the rate calculation, and how the way you extract money from your company changes everything.

If you would rather hand this to a specialist, our affordable monthly accounting packages for contractor limited companies cover corporation tax returns, salary and dividends planning, and unlimited support from a team rated in the top 1% of thousands of UK accountants.

What Is Corporation Tax and Does It Apply to Your Contractor Limited Company?

Corporation Tax is a tax on the profits of a limited company. If you operate through a personal service company or any other contractor limited company structure, your company is a separate legal entity from you as an individual - and that company pays Corporation Tax on its taxable profits each year.

This is distinct from the income tax and National Insurance you pay personally on salary or dividends you draw from the company. The company pays Corporation Tax first, on what it earns. You then pay personal taxes on what you take out. Understanding that two-stage process is the foundation of everything else in this guide.

Corporation Tax applies to trading profits, investment income, and capital gains made by the company. For most contractor limited companies, the relevant figure is trading profit: your contract income minus your allowable business expenses and any salary paid to directors or employees.

Corporation Tax Rates for Contractors in 2026/27: The 19%, 25%, and Marginal Relief Explained

What is the corporation tax rate for contractor limited companies in 2026/27?

There is no single flat rate. HMRC applies Corporation Tax at three effective levels depending on your company's taxable profits. The Small Profits Rate of 19% applies to profits up to £50,000. The Main Rate of 25% applies to profits above £250,000. Between those two thresholds, Marginal Relief applies, producing an effective rate that rises gradually from 19% towards 25%.

For a typical outside-IR35 contractor earning £80,000 to £150,000 in contract income and drawing a modest salary, taxable profits often fall in the £30,000 to £80,000 range after expenses and salary. That means many contractors sit either in the Small Profits Rate band or in the Marginal Relief zone - not at the full 25% Main Rate that often gets quoted.

Marginal Relief is calculated using a specific HMRC formula and reduces the effective rate for companies with profits between £50,000 and £250,000. It is worth understanding because it means a contractor with £60,000 of taxable profit does not suddenly pay 25% on everything - the relief tapers the rate upward gradually.

One important caveat: if you have associated companies (for example, you hold shares in another trading company), the £50,000 and £250,000 thresholds are divided between those companies. A contractor with one associated company would see the Small Profits Rate threshold drop to £25,000. This catches more contractors than you might expect.

How IR35 Status Changes Your Corporation Tax Bill

Do contractors inside IR35 still pay corporation tax?

This is the question no competitor article answers clearly, so let us be direct: yes, a company inside IR35 can still owe Corporation Tax - but in practice, the bill is often negligible or zero. Here is why.

When a contract is caught by IR35 (or the Off-Payroll Working Rules for public sector and medium-to-large private sector engagements), the income from that contract is treated as a deemed salary for tax purposes. The client or their agency deducts PAYE income tax and National Insurance at source before paying your limited company. Your company receives the net amount after those deductions.

The deemed salary calculation under IR35 allows your company to deduct a 5% allowance for business expenses (removed for public sector engagements in 2017 and for medium and large private-sector clients in April 2021, so it now only applies where your client is small and your company works out the deemed payment itself), employer's National Insurance, and pension contributions before arriving at the deemed employment payment. That deemed payment is then treated as a salary cost in your company's accounts. Because it is a deductible expense, it reduces your company's taxable profit - often to zero or close to it.

The practical result: an inside-IR35 contractor typically has very little taxable profit left in the company after the deemed salary is processed. Corporation Tax liability is minimal. But the personal tax burden is much higher, because the deemed salary is taxed at income tax rates rather than the more tax-efficient combination of salary and dividends available to outside-IR35 contractors.

This is the IR35 trap that many contractors miss. A lower Corporation Tax bill inside IR35 is not a tax saving. It reflects the fact that the profit has been reclassified as employment income and taxed more heavily at the personal level. For a detailed breakdown of how the Off-Payroll Working Rules operate, HMRC's guidance on understanding off-payroll working is the authoritative starting point.

Outside IR35, your company retains full control over its taxable profit. You decide how much salary to pay (which reduces profit), how much to contribute to a pension (which reduces profit further), and how much to leave in the company or distribute as dividends. That flexibility is where the real tax planning happens.

What Counts as Taxable Profit? Allowable Expenses Every Contractor Should Know

Taxable profit is not your contract income. It is your contract income minus all allowable business expenses. Getting this right is one of the most direct ways to reduce your Corporation Tax bill before you even think about salary or dividends planning.

Allowable expenses for contractor limited companies typically include: accountancy fees, professional indemnity and public liability insurance, home office costs (where you work from home), travel and subsistence for business purposes (subject to the 24-month rule for temporary workplaces), professional subscriptions and training directly relevant to your work, software and equipment used for the business, and marketing costs.

Salary paid to a director or employee is also a deductible expense. This is the mechanism that makes salary and dividends planning so powerful - a salary reduces the company's taxable profit, which reduces Corporation Tax, before the remaining profit is distributed as dividends and taxed at dividend rates personally.

What is not allowable: personal expenses, client entertainment (HMRC does not allow a deduction for entertaining clients, even if it is genuinely business-related), and costs that are not wholly and exclusively for business purposes. Getting the boundary wrong in either direction costs money - either you pay more Corporation Tax than necessary, or you claim expenses that trigger an HMRC enquiry.

Salary vs Dividends: How Your Profit Extraction Strategy Affects Corporation Tax

How does salary and dividend planning affect my corporation tax bill?

This is where outside-IR35 contractors have a genuine advantage - and where the right planning makes a measurable difference to your overall tax position.

Salary is a deductible expense for the company. Every pound of salary you pay yourself reduces the company's taxable profit by one pound, which reduces Corporation Tax. But salary is subject to income tax and National Insurance (both employee and employer contributions), so the personal tax cost is higher.

Dividends are paid from post-tax profit. They do not reduce Corporation Tax - the company has already paid tax on the profit before distributing it. But dividends are taxed at lower rates than salary at the personal level, and they are not subject to National Insurance. The Dividend Allowance (currently £500 per year) means the first £500 of dividends is tax-free.

The optimal strategy for most outside-IR35 contractors is a low salary (typically set at or just above the National Insurance Lower Earnings Limit, or up to the Personal Allowance threshold) combined with dividends for the remainder of profit extraction. The salary reduces Corporation Tax; the dividends are taxed efficiently at the personal level. The exact split depends on your total income, whether you have other income sources, and whether you are approaching the 40% income tax threshold.

When and How to File Your Corporation Tax Return as a Contractor

When do I need to file and pay corporation tax as a limited company contractor?

There are two separate deadlines, and confusing them is a common and costly mistake. Your Corporation Tax payment is due nine months and one day after the end of your company's accounting period. Your Corporation Tax Return (the CT600 form filed with HMRC) is due twelve months after the end of your accounting period.

So if your company's accounting year ends on 31 March 2026, your Corporation Tax payment is due by 1 January 2027, and your CT600 must be filed by 31 March 2027. You pay before you file. Missing the payment deadline triggers interest charges; missing the filing deadline triggers automatic penalties starting at £200.

Before you can file, your company must be registered for Corporation Tax with HMRC. This must be done within three months of starting to trade. HMRC will then issue a Unique Taxpayer Reference (UTR) for the company, which is required for all Corporation Tax filings. The CT600 must be filed online and must be accompanied by your company's statutory accounts.

The Low Incomes Tax Reform Group's guidance on contractors using a limited company provides a useful overview of the compliance obligations that come with operating through a limited company, including Corporation Tax registration.

Five Legal Ways to Reduce Your Corporation Tax Bill as a Limited Company Contractor

These are not loopholes. They are the legitimate planning tools available to every contractor limited company, used correctly and within HMRC's rules.

Pension contributions: Employer pension contributions made by your company are a deductible business expense. They reduce taxable profit pound for pound, with no National Insurance cost. A contractor contributing £10,000 per year into a pension through their company saves £1,900 in Corporation Tax at the Small Profits Rate, or up to £2,500 at the Main Rate - while building retirement savings.

Timing of expenses: If you know you will incur a significant business expense (new equipment, training, professional fees), incurring it before your accounting year-end rather than after brings the deduction into the current year's tax calculation. This does not eliminate the tax - it defers it - but deferral has real cash flow value.

Salary optimisation: As covered above, setting your director's salary at the right level reduces taxable profit without triggering unnecessary National Insurance. The optimal salary level changes each tax year as thresholds shift, so this needs reviewing annually.

Research and Development (R&D) relief: Contractors in technology, engineering, or scientific fields may qualify for R&D tax credits if their work involves resolving genuine technical uncertainty. The rules changed significantly in April 2024, but qualifying companies can still claim relief on qualifying expenditure, mainly as a 20% taxable expenditure credit under the merged scheme (enhanced deductions are now limited to loss-making, R&D-intensive SMEs).

Capital allowances: Equipment purchased for business use - computers, specialist tools, office furniture - qualifies for capital allowances, which reduce taxable profit. The Annual Investment Allowance allows most small companies to deduct the full cost of qualifying assets in the year of purchase rather than spreading the deduction over several years.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I reduce corporation tax as a contractor?

The most effective legal methods are employer pension contributions (which reduce taxable profit directly), optimising your director's salary to the right level (reducing profit without triggering excess National Insurance), claiming all allowable business expenses correctly, and timing significant purchases before your accounting year-end. For contractors with profits above £50,000, salary and dividends planning becomes particularly important because it affects both the Corporation Tax calculation and your personal tax position simultaneously. A good specialist contractor accountant will review pre-year end and post year-end.

What is the corporation tax rate for contractor limited companies in 2026/27?

The Small Profits Rate of 19% applies to taxable profits up to £50,000. The Main Rate of 25% applies to profits above £250,000. Between those thresholds, Marginal Relief applies, producing an effective rate that rises gradually between 19% and 25%. Most contractors with profits in the £30,000 to £80,000 range will pay either the 19% rate or an effective rate in the low-to-mid 20s through Marginal Relief. If you hold shares in associated companies, the thresholds are divided between those companies, which can push you into a higher effective rate sooner than expected.

Do contractors inside IR35 still pay corporation tax?

Technically yes, but in practice the Corporation Tax bill for an inside-IR35 contractor is usually negligible or zero. This is because the deemed salary calculation under the Off-Payroll Working Rules treats most of the contract income as employment income, which is processed through PAYE before reaching the company. The deemed salary is a deductible expense in the company's accounts, which eliminates most or all of the taxable profit. However, this is not a tax saving - the income is simply taxed more heavily at the personal level through income tax and National Insurance rather than through Corporation Tax and dividend tax.

When do I need to file and pay corporation tax as a limited company contractor?

Your Corporation Tax payment is due nine months and one day after the end of your company's accounting period. Your Corporation Tax Return (CT600) must be filed with HMRC within twelve months of the end of your accounting period. These are two separate deadlines: you pay before you file. Missing the payment deadline triggers interest charges from HMRC; missing the filing deadline triggers automatic financial penalties. Your company must also be registered for Corporation Tax with HMRC within three months of starting to trade, before any of these deadlines become relevant.

How does salary and dividend planning affect my corporation tax bill?

Salary paid to a director is a deductible expense that reduces the company's taxable profit and therefore its Corporation Tax liability. Dividends, by contrast, are paid from post-tax profit and do not reduce Corporation Tax. The optimal strategy for most outside-IR35 contractors is a low salary (reducing Corporation Tax) combined with dividends for the remainder of profit extraction (taxed at lower personal rates than salary). The exact split depends on your total income, the 40% income tax threshold, and whether you have other income sources. Getting this wrong in either direction - too high a salary or too low - costs money, which is why annual salary and dividends planning is included in specialist contractor accounting packages.
